criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Memo identifies LTV exceeds 80% FFIEC supervisory limit
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum repeatedly identifies the as-is LTV as 81.04%, but it compares that figure only to a “customary 65%--75% range” and does not state that it exceeds the 80% FFIEC/12 CFR Part 365 supervisory LTV limit for commercial real estate loans. Therefore the specific regulatory threshold required by the criterion is not identified.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Memo recommends board exception approval for LTV exceedance
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo repeatedly addresses the need to document exceptions to underwriting guidelines, including references to the bank's 'loan committee or board' approving exceptions and written confirmation of 'loan committee or board exceptions.' It also identifies the as-is LTV as 81.04%, which exceeds the 80% threshold, and notes the LTV 'runs a little hot.' This satisfies the criterion's requirement to recommend or note board/exception documentation for the LTV exceedance.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Mortgage includes specific CREC covenant for vapor barrier
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage specifically defines the SCDHEC LUR recorded in Deed Book 1203 at Page 89 and the Vapor Barrier beneath Bay 1/Lot 7, and it includes an express covenant in Section 7.1(a)-(g) requiring Borrower to maintain, protect, inspect, and not disturb the Vapor Barrier without SCDHEC approval and Lender notice/consent, along with related renovation and default provisions.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Mortgage prohibits residential conversion of ground floor Lot 7/Bay 1
criteria_results.reasoning: The output contains multiple express covenants prohibiting residential use or conversion of the ground floor of Lot 7/Bay 1, consistent with the SCDHEC LUR. Specifically, Section 7.1(c) requires Borrower to 'not use, or permit the use of, the ground floor of Lot 7 (Bay 1) for any residential purpose, and not consent to any change in the use or occupancy of Bay 1 that is inconsistent with the LUR'; Section 9.4(b) (Negative Covenants — Change of Use) prohibits use of the ground floor of Lot 7 for residential purposes or any use prohibited by the LUR; and Section 4.8 (Leasing Restrictions) bars leasing Bay 1 for residential use or permitting any change in use that would violate the LUR. The LUR definition in Section 1.1 expressly recites the residential-use prohibition, Section 3.4 represents that current use of Bay 1 is consistent with the LUR, Exhibit B (Permitted Exception 3) restates the restriction, and Section 14.1(l) and (p) make breach of the LUR/change of use an Event of Default. The prohibition is thus squarely and repeatedly included.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Breach of CREC/environmental restriction is an event of default
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly makes failure to comply with the SCDHEC land use restriction an Event of Default. Section 14.1(l) defines an Environmental Default to include breach of Section 7.1 or violation of/failure to comply with the LUR, penetration or disturbance of the Vapor Barrier without required approvals, and modification of the LUR without Lender consent. Section 7.1 separately requires Vapor Barrier maintenance and prohibits residential use of Bay 1 on Lot 7, consistent with the LUR.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Memo identifies CREC compliance obligation as a drafting issue
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum's Part III.B is devoted to the environmental issue. B.1 expressly identifies the CREC on Lot 7, the vapor barrier beneath the Bay 1 slab, and the SCDHEC land use restriction (Deed Book 1203, Page 89), and explains that the Term Sheet's general Environmental Indemnity language is insufficient. It then describes the specific covenants the draft Mortgage adds in Section 7.1 — annual vapor barrier inspection by a qualified professional at Borrower's expense, no slab penetration without SCDHEC approval and Lender notice, prohibition on residential use of Bay 1, five-day notice of SCDHEC communications, and no modification of the LUR without Lender consent — plus a corresponding Event of Default in Section 14.1(l). B.3 further adds construction draw conditions protecting the vapor barrier, and B.5 requires the SCDHEC file. The memo also flags the CREC/NFA status, the risk of reopening Site ID SC-29403-0772, and the title commitment's Requirement 6. This goes well beyond a standard environmental compliance clause and satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Memo identifies renovation holdback gap ($900K shortfall)
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly states the renovation budget total as $3,150,000 and separately identifies the Renovation Holdback of $2,250,000 and the Borrower equity allocation of $900,000 in Part V, Check 5. It also references the 71.43% holdback ratio and the $900,000 equity allocation in D.8/D.10. This sufficiently identifies that the holdback is $900,000 short of the total renovation budget and that the shortfall is funded by Borrower equity.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Mortgage requires borrower equity contribution before holdback draws
criteria_results.reasoning: The renovation disbursement provisions do not expressly require Borrower to fund its $900,000 equity contribution before Lender disburses from the Renovation Holdback, nor do they require deposit into a controlled account. Section 12.4(e)(iv) merely conditions disbursement on Borrower not having failed to fund equity 'when required,' but the timing is undefined. Exhibit C Part 4 is expressly illustrative and non-binding and shows concurrent draws rather than equity-first sequencing. Thus the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Memo flags draw schedule shows interspersed (not equity-first) funding
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum addresses the renovation draw schedule only in Section D.8, which flags a $5,000 overrun (borrower equity of $905,000 against a $900,000 allocation and a $3,155,000 cumulative total against a $3,150,000 budget). It does not state that the draw schedule intersperses borrower equity contributions with lender draws rather than requiring equity to be funded first, nor does it note the resulting risk that the renovation holdback could be exhausted before completion. No other section (D.5, D.10, Part IV, or the Priority Register) raises this sequencing concern. The criterion is therefore not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Memo identifies Harmon & Wren ROFR on Bay 2 conflict with leasing covenants
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum's Section C.4 ('The Bay 2 right of first refusal is not a title exception and does not appear in the Term Sheet at all') expressly identifies that Harmon & Wren Design Studio holds a ROFR on Bay 2 — described as vacant space being marketed in the Vacancy Schedule — and states that the ROFR 'constrains the Bank's principal lease-up lever: a third-party offer for Bay 2 must first be presented to Harmon & Wren,' and that 'The Term Sheet's DSCR covenant and its leasing covenant (Section 10.6) do not acknowledge it.' It further notes the ROFR adds 60–90 days to absorption/lease-up and that 'If the Bank intends to enforce any lease-up benchmark, that benchmark must be set with the ROFR in mind.' The Priority Register also cross-references the ROFR-constrained lease-up (Part IV item 3, Section 11.6 leasing reporting). This squarely satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Mortgage addresses ROFR in leasing covenant provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly acknowledges and accommodates the Harmon & Wren ROFR on Bay 2 in multiple places: Section 4.5(e) discloses the ROFR as a right to lease only (not a right to purchase); Section 4.8's leasing covenant prohibition is limited to options/rights of first refusal to *purchase*, so it does not conflict with the existing leasing ROFR; and Section 4.9 is a dedicated covenant ('Right of First Refusal — Bay 2') requiring Borrower to comply with and not circumvent the ROFR, with notice/copy obligations to Lender. The ROFR is also listed as a Permitted Exception (Exhibit B, Item 5), disclosed in the rent roll exhibit (Exhibit D), and its status is a required lease-up reporting item under Section 11.6. This satisfies the criterion—the existing ROFR is acknowledged, carved out from the standard leasing restrictions, and compliance is required.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Memo identifies missing assignment consent clause in Lowcountry Provisions lease
criteria_results.reasoning: Part III, Section C.3 explicitly identifies that the Lowcountry Provisions lease for Bay 1 'has no assignment or subletting provision at all' and describes it as 'the most important lease issue in the deal.' It quotes the rent roll/lease abstract confirming the lease 'is silent on assignment or subletting rights and does not contain a consent requirement, prohibition, or landlord approval mechanism,' and discusses the implications for the lender's assignment of rents—i.e., that the statutory assignment is enforceable against the tenant on notification, but the tenant may resist or litigate at enforcement and has no contractual obligation to deliver an estoppel. It also implements a three-step treatment (representation, estoppel as non-waivable condition precedent, and lease amendment at next opportunity). This squarely satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Mortgage/memo recommends estoppel certificate from Lowcountry Provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: Both documents satisfy the criterion. The Mortgage (Section 4.7(a)-(c)) makes tenant estoppel certificates a condition precedent to the Initial Advance under Term Sheet §12.1(j), expressly states Lender does not waive the condition as to the Lowcountry Lease, and adds a 90-day post-closing covenant requiring a Lowcountry estoppel that acknowledges the Mortgage and the assignment and agrees to pay Rents directly to Lender after default. The issues memorandum (Part III, Section C.3 and C.5, plus the Priority Register and closing checklist Part VII) recommends treating the Lowcountry estoppel as a hard, non-waivable closing condition to confirm the tenant's acknowledgment of the rent assignment.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Mortgage includes borrower representation re right to assign rents
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly includes a borrower representation and warranty regarding authority to assign rents. Section 4.5(b) states that Borrower has 'good right, full power and lawful authority to absolutely assign the Leases and the Rents,' including the Lowcountry Lease, and that Borrower has not previously assigned, pledged, or encumbered the Leases or Rents. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo identifies gap between SPE requirements and operating agreement
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly and extensively identifies the gap between the Term Sheet's SPE requirements and the borrower's operating agreement. Part III, Section F is dedicated to this issue: F.1 states the Operating Agreement contains no independent manager, no bankruptcy consent/remoteness provisions, and describes the required Operating Agreement Amendment as a condition precedent; F.2 notes the purpose clause is a broad catch-all and the separateness covenants are absent; F.3 notes bankruptcy is not a Major Decision. The Executive Summary (second-order finding (b)) and the Priority Register (Priority A, refs F.1–F.2) also flag that Section 6.4's SPE representation cannot be given truthfully until the Operating Agreement is amended, and Part VI/VII list the Operating Agreement Amendment as an open item and additional closing condition. This fully satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Mortgage includes SPE covenants with independent director requirement
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage includes Article VIII (Single-Purpose Entity; Separateness; Bankruptcy Remoteness), with Section 8.3 requiring that the Operating Agreement provide at all times at least one Independent Manager, whose affirmative vote is required for bankruptcy filings, receiver consent, dissolution, merger, etc.; it also includes successor appointment mechanics with a 'springing member' provision, removal restrictions requiring Lender consent, and Section 8.4 bankruptcy-remoteness covenants. This satisfies the criterion's requirement for SPE covenants with an independent director/manager (and springing member) requirement.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Memo flags need for passive member consent to SPE restrictions
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly requires the passive members' execution of and consent to the SPE-related Operating Agreement Amendment. Section F.1 states that the Amendment 'must be drafted and executed by all three Members (and by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC for Tidewater) as a condition precedent' and that it must be added to the closing checklist; Section F.4 requires Tidewater to be bound through its general partner and requires GP authority documentation; Section 6.4(c) is described as representing that the Amendment has been executed by each Member and by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC; Part VII's closing checklist adds 'Operating Agreement Amendment executed by all three Members and by Tidewater GP Holdings LLC'; and F.3 references the passive members' leverage/support. The need for passive member consent/binding is therefore clearly discussed, identifying Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP (through Tidewater GP Holdings LLC) and covering Harborline via 'all three Members.'

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Mortgage includes flood insurance covenant for $5M in Zone X
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 10.3 expressly requires Borrower to maintain flood insurance of not less than $5,000,000 and notes the Property is in FEMA Flood Zone X, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Memo or mortgage distinguishes contractual vs. regulatory flood insurance
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum (Section A.8) expressly distinguishes the $5,000,000 flood insurance requirement as a contractual Lender requirement rather than a federally mandated requirement because the Property is in FEMA Zone X, and explains that NFIP limits require private/excess coverage. The mortgage itself (Section 10.3) also states that the Property is in Zone X, that federal law does not require flood insurance there, and that the flood coverage is a contractual requirement of Lender, not a federally mandated requirement. Thus both documents satisfy the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Memo identifies balcony encroachment over King Street ROW
criteria_results.reasoning: Section A.3 of the memorandum is expressly devoted to the balcony encroachment. It states that a 2.5-foot decorative iron balcony encroaches over the King Street right-of-way, cites it as Title Commitment Schedule B-II Exception 5 and closer note 2 (insured only negatively), notes that no encroachment permit or license is in the record, requires Borrower to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain a City of Charleston license within 90 days and to procure ALTA 28.1 coverage, and flags the risk that City-ordered removal would trigger unbudgeted façade costs. It also appears in the Priority Register and Part VI/Part VII items. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Mortgage includes covenant to maintain encroachment permit/license
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.3 expressly requires Borrower to obtain and maintain in effect a valid City of Charleston encroachment license, permit, or other authorization for the balcony. Section 3.3(d) further restricts removal, alteration, or material modification of the balcony without Lender consent, which covers preventing exacerbation of the encroachment.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Yield maintenance formula specifies which U.S. Treasury rate is used
criteria_results.reasoning: The yield maintenance formula defines the 'Treasury Rate' specifically as the yield to maturity of the U.S. Treasury security reported in Federal Reserve Statistical Release H.15 under 'Treasury Constant Maturities' with a maturity closest to the last day of the Yield Maintenance Period, and provides for linear interpolation between the two nearest published Treasury Constant Maturities if no maturity is within 90 days. This satisfies the criterion by specifying which Treasury rate and maturity are used.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Yield maintenance formula includes the 50 basis point spread
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 13.3(b) of the mortgage's yield maintenance formula expressly states that the comparison interest rate is 'the Treasury Rate plus fifty (50) basis points (0.50%),' thereby including the required 50 bps spread in the yield maintenance prepayment premium calculation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Yield maintenance formula provides a calculable methodology
criteria_results.reasoning: The yield maintenance provision in Section 13.3 specifies the premium as the greater of 1.00% of outstanding principal and the present value of the excess of interest at the Applicable Rate over interest at the Treasury Rate plus 50 bps for the remaining Yield Maintenance Period. It identifies the discount rate as the Treasury Rate, defines how the Treasury Rate is determined (H.15 constant maturities, with interpolation if necessary), and describes the present-value calculation, monthly interest assumption, and 30/360 day count. This provides a sufficiently calculable methodology from the formula alone.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Memo identifies yield maintenance ambiguity in term sheet
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum extensively addresses yield maintenance ambiguity and enforceability. Section E.3 identifies an ambiguity in the Term Sheet's allocation of the 50 bps spread ('This resolves the Term Sheet's ambiguity, but the Bank should confirm'), and Section E.4 identifies an internal inconsistency in the Treasury Rate definition ("closest to but not exceeding" versus "interpolate between the two nearest") that 'cannot both be applied to the same fact pattern,' resolving it in Mortgage Section 13.3(c) by specifying the Treasury Constant Maturity series from Federal Reserve Statistical Release H.15 with precise interpolation rules. Section E.5 flags that the Note must be conformed to the Mortgage formula to avoid conflicting economics. Section E.8 expressly addresses enforceability, stating that South Carolina courts require the formula to be 'specific, mathematically deterministic, and objectively calculable' and that 'If the formula is ambiguous ... a court could deem it an unenforceable penalty,' and explains the four drafting features that support enforceability (deterministic formula, manifest-error standard, liquidated-damages recital, 1% floor). The criterion's requirements—identifying yield maintenance ambiguity (including the treasury rate definition), resolving it in the mortgage, and tying it to South Carolina penalty/enforceability risk—are all satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Mortgage transfer restrictions cover indirect/fund-level changes
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.2(c) expressly addresses indirect transfers and change of control, including any transfer of direct or indirect ownership interests in any Member or any Person controlling a Member, any change in the general partner of Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP, and any change in the manager, managing member, or Control of Harborline Capital Advisors LLC. It also captures transfers of Guarantor's interest in Graydon Development Group LLC. This satisfies the criterion for indirect/upstream change-of-control restrictions.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Memo identifies transfer restriction gap re fund-level changes
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo expressly identifies the transfer-restriction gap in Part III.H.4, concluding that neither the Term Sheet (§10.3) nor the Operating Agreement captures upstream/indirect control changes: it notes Guarantor could sell his interest in Graydon Development Group LLC (holder of the 72%) without any 'transfer of an ownership interest in Borrower' occurring, and that the Operating Agreement 'contains no change of control provision that would capture indirect or upstream transfers.' It also flags the overbroad 'transfers among existing members' exception and undefined 25% aggregate test. The draft's cure (Section 9.2(c)) expressly captures 'any change in Tidewater's general partner,' transfers by Tidewater to a 'successor fund' under Op. Agmt §4.2(c), any merger/conversion of a Member, any change in manager of Harborline, and admission of a new Member — directly addressing GP-composition and fund-level changes for Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP. Part IV item 1 repeats that the Term Sheet captures only direct membership transfers, and the Priority Register lists this as item H.4. While LP-interest transfers are not named as explicitly as GP changes, the criterion's core — that the 10%/25% language with the member exception may not capture effective control changes at the fund or upstream level — is clearly identified and analyzed.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: 'Existing members' exception is narrowly defined
criteria_results.reasoning: The transfer restriction in Section 9.2(b) narrowly defines the 'existing members' exception by expressly identifying the three existing members—Graydon Development Group LLC, Tidewater Opportunity Fund II LP, and Harborline Capital Advisors LLC—and imposes additional conditions, including no change of control and Graydon retaining at least 51% and serving as Managing Member. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Memo identifies tight timeline between completion and DSCR testing
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively addresses the timing squeeze the criterion targets, and goes further than required. It establishes the key dates: substantial completion at 14 months (June 15, 2026, §A.7, H.5) and DSCR testing commencing after month 24 (April/June 2027, §D.1, D.6). It identifies that the window between completion and the first DSCR test is the pre-stabilization period — G.1 expressly describes 'ten unguaranteed months across the pre-stabilization window,' running from July 2026 through April 2027, immediately after substantial completion and before the DSCR test, during which 'Suite B is not yet generating rent, Bay 3's renewal is unresolved.' D.6 notes the lease-up analysis itself assumes Suite B is not stabilized by the April 15, 2027 test date, and H.8 characterizes the period as a 'two-stage lease-up' requiring quarterly monitoring. The memo also squarely addresses the insufficiency of current income: D.1 states in-place NOI of ~$320,100 yields 0.37x interest-only / 0.28x amortizing, and that even best-case fully stabilized NOI ($622,772) yields only 0.72x/0.55x against the 1.25x covenant — i.e., the covenant cannot be met even if lease-up were complete by the test date. The precise arithmetic '24 − 14 = 10 months' is not stated as a standalone sentence, but every element of the concern (completion date vs. test date gap, pre-stabilization lease-up window, and insufficient in-place income) is expressly analyzed and flagged as Priority A. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Mortgage includes DSCR cure mechanism or cash sweep provision
criteria_results.reasoning: The DSCR covenant in Section 11.1 includes protective mechanisms rather than only a hard default. First, Section 11.1(c) requires the DSCR to fall below the 1.25x covenant for two consecutive Test Periods before an Event of Default arises, providing a cushion. Second, and more importantly, Section 11.1(d) imposes a distribution lock-up/cash-trap style restriction: Borrower may not make any distribution to any Member during any period in which the DSCR is below 1.10x (other than permitted tax distributions). This is a protective provision tied to DSCR deterioration that restricts cash leakage to equity holders, analogous to a cash sweep/cash trap. While there is no express equity cure right or additional reserve deposit (and Section 11.1(c)'s cross-reference to a cure under Section 14.3(d) is imperfect since 14.3(d) actually provides no cure period), the mortgage does contain a genuine protective mechanism addressing DSCR shortfalls, so it does not present a bare hard default with no protective provision.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Memo identifies chain of title concern for vacated Anson Lane strip

The memo also recommends confirming title insurance coverage: it directs obtaining written confirmation from Prestige Title on extended-coverage premium, any limiting endorsements, and ALTA 34 availability; Section 3.2 of the draft mortgage requires Borrower to deliver a clean policy or endorsement for Parcel Two, and the issue appears again in the Executive Summary and Priority Register (A.1). The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Mortgage legal description includes Anson Lane strip

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes renovation reserve/holdback of $2,250,000

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes initial advance of $12,500,000 at closing

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes absolute assignment of rents (not collateral assignment)
criteria_results.reasoning: Article IV is expressly titled 'ABSOLUTE ASSIGNMENT OF LEASES, RENTS AND PROFITS,' and Section 4.1 states that Borrower 'unconditionally, absolutely and presently' assigns the Leases and Rents, expressly providing that the assignment 'shall be construed as an absolute and present assignment of the Leases and Rents and not merely a collateral assignment or an assignment as additional security.' Section 4.2 invokes the South Carolina Uniform Assignment of Rents Act (UARAA), addresses perfection upon recording, and enforcement upon default, with Sections 4.3–4.4 providing the customary revocable license/notice mechanics. The only use of 'collateral assignment' language is in Section 2.4, which applies to the GC Contract and design professional agreements, not to leases and rents. The characterization is unambiguous and consistent with SC law.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage grants security interest in personal property and UCC collateral
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly grants a first-priority security interest in personal property, fixtures, equipment, accounts, general intangibles, and other UCC collateral. Article V contains a security agreement and fixture filing, and Section 5.3 expressly authorizes filing a UCC-1 financing statement with the South Carolina Secretary of State covering the Personal Property Collateral. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes security interest in permits, licenses, and development rights
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly includes permits, licenses, entitlements, and development rights as part of the Mortgaged Property. criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes security interest in contracts and project documents
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly includes contracts, warranties, guarantees, and project documents as collateral. The granting clause covers general intangibles, warranties, guaranties, indemnities, and all rights under the GC Contract, defined as the construction contract with Beaufort Builders Group LLC. Section 2.4 further collaterally assigns the GC Contract, design professional agreements, warranties, guaranties, surety bonds, and indemnities relating to the renovation.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes covenant against subordinate financing without consent
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 9.1 ("No Subordinate Financing") of the mortgage expressly prohibits Borrower from incurring, creating, assuming, or permitting to exist any lien, mortgage, deed of trust, security interest, pledge, encumbrance, subordinate or mezzanine financing, preferred equity, or participating interest affecting the Property without Lender's prior written consent in each instance. It further bars any financing statement naming Borrower as debtor covering the Mortgaged Property other than those for Lender. This is reinforced by Section 3.1(f) (no further mortgaging or pledging) and Section 9.5 (limits on additional indebtedness). The covenant against subordinate financing/additional liens without lender consent is clearly present.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes transfer restriction with 10% individual / 25% aggregate thresholds
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage includes Section 9.2(b), which expressly restricts transfers of direct membership interests in Borrower if any Person or group would acquire more than 10% in a single transaction or series, or if transfers aggregate more than 25%, in each case without Lender's prior written consent.

criteria_results.title: SPE covenant: borrower restricted to owning/operating the Property only
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage includes an express SPE covenant in Section 8.1 stating that Borrower's sole purpose is to acquire, own, manage, lease, renovate, operate, finance, refinance, and dispose of the Property and related incidental activities, and that Borrower shall not engage in any other business or activity. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: SPE covenant: no voluntary bankruptcy without independent director consent
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage includes an express SPE covenant in Article VIII. Section 8.3 requires at least one Independent Manager and mandates the Independent Manager's affirmative vote, consent, or approval before Borrower may file a voluntary bankruptcy petition or take similar insolvency actions. Section 8.4 further reinforces this bankruptcy-remoteness requirement. Thus the criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: SPE covenant: separate books and no commingling
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 8.2 (Separateness Covenants) expressly requires Borrower to "maintain its own separate books of account, financial records, bank accounts... separate and apart from those of any other Person" (clause (a)) and to "not commingle its funds or assets with those of any Affiliate, Member, manager or other Person" (clause (b)). Both required SPE provisions—separate books/records and no commingling with affiliates—are present, reinforced by Section 8.1 (Single-Purpose Status) and the remedies in Section 14.1(j).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Yield maintenance enforceability under SC law discussed
criteria_results.reasoning: Part III, Section E.8 is expressly captioned 'Enforceability: characterize the premium carefully, and keep the formula deterministic,' and discusses South Carolina courts' treatment of yield maintenance premiums, the requirement that the formula be specific, mathematically deterministic and objectively calculable, and the risk that an ambiguous formula could be deemed an unenforceable penalty. It also enumerates four drafting features supporting enforceability (deterministic formula, 'manifest error' standard, liquidated-damages recital, small 1% floor) and advises against characterizing the premium as a 'fee' or 'additional interest.' Related discussion appears in E.7 (SC penalty scrutiny on acceleration), E.1 (1% floor supporting the reasonable-estimate characterization), and H.6/I.2 (recommending a South Carolina opinion covering enforceability of the yield maintenance formula). The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: SC Assignment of Rents Act referenced for rent assignment

Code § 29-3-100 et seq.)', explaining why the section citation was deliberately omitted from the recorded instrument pending verification. Either document alone satisfies the criterion, and both do.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes environmental indemnity or reference to separate environmental indemnity
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage expressly references a separate Environmental Indemnity Agreement. Section 1.1 defines "Environmental Indemnity" as "that certain Environmental Indemnity Agreement of even date herewith executed by Borrower and Guarantor in favor of Lender." It is also listed among the "Loan Documents" in Section 1.1, referenced in Section 16.1 (recourse/carve-outs governed by the Note, Guaranty and Environmental Indemnity), Section 16.2 (Guarantor's obligations under the Environmental Indemnity), Section 14.1(f) (cross-default under the Environmental Indemnity), Section 15.1(f) (remedies under the Environmental Indemnity), and in the Guarantor Consent and Acknowledgment. The mortgage additionally contains substantive environmental covenants and conditions (Article VII, Section 7.1) regarding the CREC, LUR and Vapor Barrier. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage addresses condemnation/eminent domain proceedings
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage includes Section 10.8 (Condemnation), which requires Borrower to notify Lender of condemnation/eminent-domain proceedings, assigns all condemnation awards and compensation to Lender, appoints Lender as attorney-in-fact to collect them, and gives Lender the right to apply awards to restoration or to the Obligations, with acceleration rights if the taking renders the Property unsuitable. Condemnation awards are also assigned in the granting clause (paragraph (f)) and addressed in Sections 13.5 and 15.4. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Mortgage includes casualty/damage provisions and insurance proceeds application
criteria_results.reasoning: The mortgage contains a full Article X on Insurance, including Section 10.1 (all-risk property insurance, mortgagee/loss payee clauses, ordinance or law coverage), Section 10.4 (builder's risk during renovation), and crucially Section 10.7 'Application of Insurance Proceeds,' which gives Lender the election to apply insurance proceeds either to restoration of the Improvements or to payment of the Obligations, sets conditions under which proceeds must be made available for restoration (no default, full coverage, restoration feasible within 12 months, sufficient funds), requires disbursement through the Article XII draw procedures, addresses non-restoration application without prepayment premium, and appoints Lender as attorney-in-fact to endorse and collect proceeds. Section 10.8 similarly assigns condemnation awards and gives Lender the election to apply them to restoration or debt, and Section 10.9 permits Lender to obtain insurance at Borrower's expense as a Protective Advance. Article XIV (14.1(g)) and Section 1.1 also treat insurance proceeds as part of the Mortgaged Property/proceeds collateral. Casualty and proceeds-application provisions are therefore clearly present and comprehensive.
